title: The Full State Pension Is Now £22 From Being Taxed 😳👴 #shorts
description:
The full new State Pension is £22 a year from being taxed.

In 2016/17 the full new State Pension was £155.65 a week (£8,093.80 a year), nearly £3,000 below the £11,000 tax-free Personal Allowance. Since then it has gone up 55%, to £241.30 a week (£12,547.60 a year) in 2026/27. Prices (CPI) rose about 44% from April 2016 to September 2026. That's the triple lock: the State Pension rises each year by the highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5%.

But the tax-free allowance has been frozen at £12,570 since April 2021, and stays there until April 2031. So the full new State Pension is now £22.40 a year below it, and one more rise takes it over the line.

The good news: at Budget 2025 the government said pensioners whose only income is the basic or new State Pension (without extra amounts) won't have to pay that small amount of tax from 2027-28, and a minister later said they "will not have to pay income tax over this Parliament". Details are due at the Budget on 28 October 2026. If you have other income too (a workplace or private pension, say), the State Pension already counts towards your tax.

Sources: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/524117/benefit-and-pension-rates-from-6-april-2016.pdf · https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/benefit-and-pension-rates-2026-to-2027/proposed-benefit-and-pension-rates-2026-to-2027 · https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/tax-and-tax-credit-rates-and-thresholds-for-2016-17/tax-and-tax-credit-rates-and-thresholds-for-2016-17 · https://www.gov.uk/income-tax-rates · https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/maintaining-income-tax-and-equivalent-national-insurance-contributions-thresholds-until-5-april-2031 · ONS CPI D7BT: https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/timeseries/d7bt/mm23 · Triple lock: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/huge-income-boost-for-millions-of-pensioners-and-working-people · House of Commons Library, Taxation of state pension (CBP-10250): https://researchbriefings.files.parliament.uk/documents/CBP-10250/CBP-10250.pdf · https://www.gov.uk/guidance/how-your-state-pension-is-taxed

facts.how: 2016/17 tax year: first year of the new State Pension (£155.65 a week)
ONS CPI D7BT 144.1 (Sep 2026) ÷ 100.2 (Apr 2016) − 1 = 43.8%, 'about 44%', arithmetic in scenes.py

assumptions: A year = 52 weeks of the full new State Pension (for people reaching State Pension age from 6 April 2016); the full basic State Pension is lower (£184.90 a week in 2026/27).
'Prices' = ONS CPI index from April 2016 to September 2026 (latest month, released 21 Oct 2026).
Triple lock (spoken as 'two and a half per cent'): highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5% (gov.uk). Not in law as a floor; a government commitment for this Parliament (Budget 2025).
'One more rise crosses the line': any rise above 0.18% (£22.40 ÷ £12,547.60) takes £241.30 × 52 above £12,570 while the allowance is frozen to April 2031.

'You won't pay that tax': Budget 2025 para 4.167 and the Exchequer Secretary (Jan 2026), as reported by the House of Commons Library (CBP-10250, 22 Sep 2026); applies to people whose only income is the basic or new State Pension without increments; details due at the Budget on 28 Oct 2026.
